title: Why Power Query
summary: Power Query gets data, cleans it in recorded steps and loads the result, without touching the source. Next month you click Refresh and every step runs again on the new data.
objectives: Explain what Power Query does: get, transform, load, then refresh.
Open the Power Query Editor from a Table and find the ribbon, preview, formula bar and Applied Steps.
Remove a column and filter rows, and see each click become a step.
Close & Load the result, and refresh it when the source changes.

slides.h: Every month, the same forty minutes
p: On the 1st of every month Ishaan exports the sales, deletes the notes column, removes cancelled invoices, fixes the dates and pastes the rest into the report. Same clicks, every month, and one slip spoils the numbers.
Manual steps leave no record: nobody can see what was done.
A missed filter is invisible until the totals look odd.
Power Query records the steps once and repeats them for you.
In real life: once pasted April’s data over May’s. The report went to the directors before anyone noticed.

p: Power Query does three things. It gets data from a source, transforms it with steps you click, and loads the clean result into Excel. The source itself never changes.
It’s in every Excel since 2016 under **Data › Get & Transform Data**.
Older guides call it “Get & Transform”; it’s the same tool.
Power BI uses the same engine, so what you learn here carries over.
In real life: asked for “the same report, every month, by the 2nd”. Power Query is how Ishaan now says yes.

terms: Excel’s tool for getting, cleaning and combining data in recorded steps
one set of steps that turns a source into a table

items: a Table, a CSV file, a workbook, a folder
steps you click in the editor
a Table on a sheet, or the Data Model
every step runs again on new data

p: Every click in the editor becomes a step in Applied Steps. Together they’re a recipe: the same ingredients in, the same dish out. Next month, new ingredients, same recipe.
Click a step to see the data as it was at that point.
Each step reads the one before it.
Delete a step with its ✕; the steps after it carry on.
In real life: showed Neha the Applied Steps instead of explaining his spreadsheet. She read it like a checklist.

slides.h: Open the editor from a Table
p: Click any cell in the Table, then Data › From Table/Range. Excel opens the Power Query Editor with two steps already there: Source, which reads the Table, and Changed Type, which guesses each column’s type.
If the range isn’t a Table yet, Excel offers to make it one first.
The query is named after the Table.
Nothing changes on your sheet until you load.
In real life: keeps the raw export on a sheet called Raw and never types on it again.

callouts.text: Formula bar: the step in M

p: Select the Notes column and choose Remove Columns. A step called Removed Columns appears, and the formula bar shows what it does in M, Power Query’s formula language.
You don’t have to write M: the buttons write it.
Reading it tells you exactly what a step does.
Turn the formula bar on with View › Formula Bar if it’s hidden.
In real life: doesn’t read M, but she can see “RemoveColumns … Notes” and knows what it means.

p: Home › Close & Load puts the result on a new sheet as a Table, named after the query. When the source changes, Data › Refresh All runs the query again and the Table updates.
The Queries & Connections pane lists every query and how many rows it loaded.
Refresh All (Ctrl+Alt+F5) refreshes every query in the workbook.
Right-click the result › Refresh for just that one.
In real life: now adds the month’s rows to Raw, clicks Refresh All, and goes for chai.

lab.intro: Dhanush’s May sales are in the Table **Sales** on the **Raw** sheet. The query **Sales** is open in the Power Query Editor with its first two steps. Clean it for Neha’s report.

hints: Click the Notes column header to select it.
Home › Remove Columns, or right-click the header › Remove.
tasks.solution:
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    #"Changed Type" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source,{{"Invoice", type text}, {"Date", type datetime}, {"Branch", type text}, {"Customer", type text}, {"Item", type text}, {"Qty", Int64.Type}, {"Rate", Int64.Type}, {"Status", type text}, {"Notes", type text}}),
    #"Removed Columns" = Table.RemoveColumns(#"Changed Type",{"Notes"})
in
    #"Removed Columns"
tasks.explain: Select **Notes**, then Home › Remove Columns. Power Query writes `Table.RemoveColumns(#"Changed Type",{"Notes"})`.
tasks.ref:
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    #"Changed Type" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source,{{"Invoice", type text}, {"Date", type datetime}, {"Branch", type text}, {"Customer", type text}, {"Item", type text}, {"Qty", Int64.Type}, {"Rate", Int64.Type}, {"Status", type text}, {"Notes", type text}}),
    #"Removed Columns" = Table.RemoveColumns(#"Changed Type",{"Notes"})
in
    #"Removed Columns"

tasks.prompt: Remove the **Cancelled** invoices: keep every other status.
hints: Use the ▾ filter button on the Status header.
Untick Cancelled, leave the others ticked.
tasks.solution:
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    #"Changed Type" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source,{{"Invoice", type text}, {"Date", type datetime}, {"Branch", type text}, {"Customer", type text}, {"Item", type text}, {"Qty", Int64.Type}, {"Rate", Int64.Type}, {"Status", type text}, {"Notes", type text}}),
    #"Removed Columns" = Table.RemoveColumns(#"Changed Type",{"Notes"}),
    #"Filtered Rows" = Table.SelectRows(#"Removed Columns", each ([Status] <> "Cancelled"))
in
    #"Filtered Rows"
tasks.explain: Status ▾ › untick **Cancelled** › OK. Power Query writes `each ([Status] <> "Cancelled")`, so any new status stays in.

tasks.prompt: **Close & Load** the query to a table on a new sheet.
hints: It’s the first button on the Home tab.
The result appears on a sheet called Sales.
tasks.okMsg: Loaded: the clean table is on its own sheet.

tasks.prompt: June’s rows are added to the **Sales** Table on Raw. How do you update the clean table?
tasks.explain: Refresh runs the same steps on the new rows. That’s the point of a query.
options: Run every step again by hand
Delete the query and start again
Copy and paste June under May

why.0: The steps are recorded; Refresh repeats them.
why.2: The query is the reusable part: keep it.
why.3: Pasting is what Power Query replaces.

tasks.prompt: After your three steps, what has happened to the **Sales** Table on the Raw sheet?
tasks.explain: Power Query never changes its source. The clean result is a new table.
options: Notes and the cancelled rows are gone from it

why.0: Those changes are in the query’s result, not the source.
why.3: The source stays, so next month’s refresh can read it.

queries.Sales:
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    #"Changed Type" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source,{{"Invoice", type text}, {"Date", type datetime}, {"Branch", type text}, {"Customer", type text}, {"Item", type text}, {"Qty", Int64.Type}, {"Rate", Int64.Type}, {"Status", type text}, {"Notes", type text}})
in
    #"Changed Type"

quiz.q: Which three things does Power Query do?
You remove a column in the editor. The source Table…
quiz.explain: Power Query reads the source; it never writes to it.

quiz.q: Where do you see every step a query takes?
quiz.explain: One line per step, in order.

quiz.q: The first two steps after From Table/Range are…
quiz.explain: Source reads the Table; Changed Type guesses the types.
The list holds the columns to drop.

quiz.q: Which keyboard shortcut refreshes every query in the workbook?
quiz.explain: Refresh All. F9 recalculates formulas, not queries.

points: Power Query **gets** data, **transforms** it in recorded steps and **loads** the result; **Refresh** repeats it on new data.
Every click is a step in **Applied Steps**; the formula bar shows its M.
The source never changes: Close & Load writes a new Table on its own sheet.
recap.cheat: Get → transform → load → refresh; every click is a step; the source never changes.
